title: Outbox, CDC, dead letters, sagas and reconciliation
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: The dual-write problem and the transactional outbox, Debezium change data capture, retries and dead-letter queues, saga styles, and reconciling data across systems.
source: microservices.io (transactional outbox, saga); Debezium documentation (outbox event router, PostgreSQL connector); Spring for Apache Kafka error handling; Designing Data-Intensive Applications; AWS prescriptive guidance on sagas

questions.prompt: A service saves an order to PostgreSQL and then publishes OrderCreated to Kafka. The process crashes between the two steps. What is the root problem the outbox pattern solves?

options.text: The database commit and the broker publish cannot be made one atomic action.
options.why: Right: a crash in between leaves a saved order with no event, or the reverse.

options.text: Kafka cannot store messages larger than the single order row that was saved in the database.
options.why: Message size is unrelated to the crash between two systems.

options.text: PostgreSQL transactions cannot contain more than one insert statement before they must commit.
options.why: Multi-statement transactions are fine; the issue is spanning two systems.

options.text: The consumer cannot deserialise the event after a crash.
options.why: Deserialisation is a different failure from the lost-event window.

questions.explanation: Dual write = two independent systems updated without a shared transaction. Outbox writes the event to a table in the same local transaction, and a relay publishes it afterwards.

questions.prompt: Tables orders(id, customer_id, total) and outbox(id serial, aggregate_id, event_type, payload jsonb, published_at). In ONE transaction insert order 7 for customer 3 with total 99.50 and an outbox row of type OrderCreated for aggregate 7 with payload {"orderId": 7}. Write the SQL.
questions.explanation: Either both rows are committed or neither is. In Spring this is one @Transactional method calling both repositories. Nothing is sent to the broker inside this transaction.

questions.prompt: A relay worker polls the outbox table. Write the query that selects up to 100 unpublished rows (published_at IS NULL) in id order, locking them so several relay instances never pick the same rows and do not block each other.

checks.label: orders by id and limits to 100

questions.model: SELECT * FROM outbox WHERE published_at IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;
questions.explanation: After publishing, the relay sets published_at (or deletes the row) in the same transaction. A crash after publishing but before that update re-sends the event, which is why the delivery is at-least-once.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: The transactional outbox gives at-least-once, not exactly-once, delivery to the broker.
questions.reason: The relay can crash after publishing an event but before marking it as published, so it publishes the same event again on restart.

whys.a: Correct: the publish and the mark-as-sent are still two steps, so a duplicate is possible and consumers must be idempotent.
whys.b: R is the mechanism behind A.

questions.explanation: Pair the outbox with an idempotent consumer keyed on the event id. Debezium-based outbox has the same at-least-once property.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Debezium and change data capture (CDC) are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: It reads the database transaction log rather than polling tables.
options.why: Right: for PostgreSQL it uses logical decoding of the WAL.

options.text: An abandoned PostgreSQL replication slot can make WAL pile up and fill the disk.
options.why: Right: the server keeps WAL until the slot's consumer confirms it, so monitor slot lag.

options.text: Debezium commonly runs as connectors on Kafka Connect.
options.why: Right: connectors emit change events to Kafka topics.

options.text: It adds no load at all to the source database.
options.why: Reading the log is light but not free: slots, WAL retention and initial snapshots all cost resources.

options.text: It delivers every change exactly once under any failure.
options.why: Delivery is at-least-once; consumers must tolerate duplicates after a restart.

questions.explanation: Debezium's outbox event router transformation turns outbox rows into events on a topic, so you avoid writing a polling relay yourself.

questions.text: Debezium streams row changes by reading the database {1}; for PostgreSQL this uses a logical replication {2}, and a stalled one makes the server keep {3} on disk.
questions.explanation: Compared with trigger-based capture and polling, log-based CDC sees every committed change in commit order with no changes to application queries.

questions.prompt: A consumer retries a failing message 3 times after the first attempt, waiting 1 s, 2 s and 4 s before the retries (exponential, multiplier 2). Ignoring processing time, how many seconds pass between the first failure and the message being sent to the dead-letter queue?
questions.explanation: 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 seconds of waiting. Retries block the partition in a simple Kafka consumer, so long backoff windows stall everything behind the message; non-blocking retry topics avoid this.

questions.prompt: One malformed record on a Kafka partition throws on every attempt and blocks everything behind it. What is the standard remedy?

options.text: Retry a bounded number of times with backoff, then publish it to a dead-letter topic and move on.
options.why: Right: bounded retries plus DLT keeps the partition moving and keeps the evidence.

options.text: Retry the same record forever with a fixed pause, so the partition stays blocked until it succeeds.
options.why: A permanently bad record never succeeds and the partition stays blocked.

options.text: Skip the record silently by committing past it, without logging or storing the failed payload anywhere. That also hides the data-quality problem from the team that owns the producer.
options.why: Silent loss hides data problems; park it somewhere inspectable instead.

options.text: Delete the whole partition and recreate the topic, accepting that every other record on it is lost.
options.why: That destroys healthy data to remove one bad record.

questions.explanation: Also distinguish retryable errors (timeouts) from non-retryable ones (deserialisation, validation), which should go straight to the DLT.

questions.prompt: Write a Spring Kafka bean method errorHandler(KafkaTemplate<Object, Object> template) returning a DefaultErrorHandler that publishes failed records to a dead-letter topic with DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer and retries 3 times, 1 second apart, using a FixedBackOff.
questions.model:
return new DefaultErrorHandler(new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(template), new FixedBackOff(1000L, 3));
}
questions.explanation: The recoverer publishes to <topic>.DLT by default. FixedBackOff(interval, maxAttempts) counts retries after the first delivery. ExponentialBackOffWithMaxRetries is another valid way to add backoff.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: A dead-letter queue needs alerting and a replay procedure, not just existence.

whys.a: Append-only storage does not explain why DLQs need alerts.
whys.b: Correct: both are true but unrelated; an unwatched DLQ is just a place where failures silently pile up.

questions.explanation: Track DLQ depth and age, include the original topic, offset and error in headers, and make replay idempotent.

questions.prompt: Match each saga term with its meaning.

right.text: Services react to each other's events with no central coordinator
A coordinator tells each participant what to do next and tracks the state
A business action that semantically undoes an earlier committed step
The step after which the saga is committed to complete going forward
A two-phase commit lock held across all services

questions.explanation: Choreography is simple for few steps but the flow is spread across services. Orchestration (Temporal, Step Functions, Camunda) centralises the flow and makes it easier to see and test.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: A saga step that already sent a confirmation email can be compensated by un-sending that email.
questions.reason: A compensation is a new forward business action (for example a correction email), not a database rollback.

whys.d: Correct: you cannot un-send an email; compensation is a new action such as sending a cancellation (R true).

questions.explanation: Order saga steps so irreversible actions come last (after the pivot), and make every compensation idempotent and retryable.

questions.prompt: Reconciling by transaction id: the ledger has 1,000 transactions, the bank statement has 998, and 4 bank transactions have no ledger match. How many ledger transactions have no match in the bank statement?
questions.explanation: Bank 998 = matched + 4 bank-only, so matched = 994. Ledger-only = 1,000 - 994 = 6.

questions.prompt: Ledger amounts are 10.00, 20.00, 30.00 and 40.00. The matching bank amounts, in the same order, are 10.004, 20.02, 29.995 and 40.50. A pair matches if the absolute difference is at most 0.01. How many pairs match?
questions.explanation: Differences are 0.004, 0.02, 0.005 and 0.50. Only the first and third are within 0.01. Use decimals or integer cents in real code, never float equality.

questions.prompt: ledger and bank are dicts of transaction id to amount. Write def reconcile(ledger, bank, tol=0.01) returning a tuple (ids only in ledger, ids only in bank, ids in both whose amounts differ by more than tol).

checks.label: finds ids present on only one side

questions.model:
only_ledger = ledger.keys() - bank.keys()
    only_bank = bank.keys() - ledger.keys()
    diff = {k for k in ledger.keys() & bank.keys() if abs(ledger[k] - bank[k]) > tol}
    return only_ledger, only_bank, diff
questions.explanation: Any loop-based version is fine. Use Decimal or integer cents for money, report all three buckets with counts and sums, and allow a grace window for late-arriving data before raising an alert.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: A reconciliation job should wait out a grace window before alarming on a transaction missing from the bank file.

whys.a: R is false so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Correct: settlement lag is real, hence the grace window (A true); R is false.

questions.explanation: Compare by event date, make the job re-runnable and idempotent so late records fix earlier mismatches, and track aging buckets for items that stay unmatched.
